The delusional mirror of the soul

Interesting - though I must bring to the table that the word 'soul' can be interpreted in different ways, and therefore the argument proposed in this article loses some weight.

For me the article talks about the soul as one would imagine the conditioned ego - what we believe to be right based upon our own life experiences up to a fixed point in time. This is not the same thing as the energy that gives us life, the personality and talents that we are born with, nor the consciousness that we experience with our birth.

Of course, these ideas I mention above, which more represent the soul to me, may also be seen and explained by others as something more scientific rather than spiritual and this for me is deluded.

Delusion only comes from situations in which we can interpret, remember or opine - these are cerebral processes - and the soul (or spirit as I prefer to call it) definitely does not simply stem from the brain.

If you define soul not as the Judeo-Christian concept as divine spark of spirit, or the Greek concept of the animating force whether animus or Logos, or the essence retained during reincarnation, but as the central ‘selfness’ that constitutes the unique you, with all the component parts, then your essence is composed not only of the nexus of the physical universe being the matter and energy network combining into one entity as the sum total of your probabilistic Schrodinger wave equation, the genetic organization with which you are endowed, but also the informational content acquired through existence. You acquire knowledge through senses and translate the stimuli to form the belief structures which become your foundation, which can include the spiritual content believed. Witness the transformations in Mahatma (Great Soul) Gandhi and St Paul on the road to Damascus. One core element in the article is that you choose which elements of your environment to subsume into your being, from the food you eat, to the concepts in which you choose to believe, to the energy you channel into your life’s actions and the ethical beliefs you construct as your guide. Even hopes of post-continuance after your dissipation can be incorporated. Consciousness is a state induced by the operation of a highly complex brain and CNS which has acquired extraordinary feedback re-entrant capability without which divine spark would be an invisible empty energy. Forming these into your core structure is performed through you exercising critical judgment of their validity, but judgment can be notorious since by its basis is subjective. This illusion of construct validity turns to delusion when you retain the structure despite evidence to the contrary you choose to ignore. “I believe” is the last recourse to maintain an untenable hypothesis, usually followed by ‘absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.’ But I do appreciate your insights.

Hi. Thanks for humouring me. It's obvious that you are far more academically inclined towards this subject than I.

However, as a layman, I would like to take this opportunity to ask your opinion on a couple of points if I may?

If I am to understand correctly, this article defines the 'soul' as an accumulation of sensual experiences, of which we choose to include in our own personal construct over the duration of our lifetime. This is the illusion that becomes delusion whenever we argue our own personal belief at any time as if it is true. I can agree with this.

However, if this is truly the case, then the idea expressed within the article is also based upon a qualitative understanding of the human condition. A subjective view that is just as likely to be delusional as anyone else's opinion. Or should we just accept this article to be the one truth that should not be looked at critically?

Again accepting the premise of the article, I also want to ask if this means that a new born baby is without a 'soul' until it learns to collect, store and recall sensory information in respect to judging any situation it may encounter in it's early days. If this is the case then I think we need to revise the word 'soul' purely on a semantic level.

Obviously when using the term 'mirror of the soul' we are talking about self reflection, and in itself this suggests the absolute mental aspect of understanding the nature of the self. And yet I cannot shake the doubt I have that we are far more than a connected bundle of nerves and complex cerebral processes. There are too many anomalies in life for this to be the case.
